ai.literal: My lord before do not stand, O enemies! Many, my lord before having stood, [are] those who stood [as] stone.
ai.translation: O enemies, do not stand against my lord! Many who stood before him are now standing as memorial stones.
ai.modern: பகைவர்களே! என் தலைவனுக்கு முன்னே போரிட நிற்காதீர்கள். அவனுக்கு முன் எதிர்த்து நின்ற பலர் இப்போது நடுகல்லாக நிற்கிறார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet is spoken by a warrior warning the enemy forces about his commander's fierce prowess in battle. The word 'என்னை' (eṉṉai) here is formed from 'என்' (my) and 'ஐ' (lord or master), meaning 'my commander', rather than the accusative pronoun 'me'. The warrior warns that many who previously dared to stand against his lord are now standing as 'கல்' (kal), referring to the hero stones erected for the dead. It vividly conveys the lethal certainty of facing this great warrior.

ai.literal: Forest hare shot than-arrow elephant missed spear holding is-sweeter.
ai.translation: Holding a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than holding an arrow that successfully hit a forest hare.
ai.modern: காட்டில் உள்ள முயலை எய்து வீழ்த்திய அம்பினை ஏந்துவதை விட, பெரிய யானை மீது எறிந்து குறி தவறிய வேலை ஏந்துவது பெருமையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts a successful but small achievement with a failed but grand ambition. Hitting a timid forest hare with an arrow requires little courage, so the success brings no real glory. In contrast, daring to attack a massive elephant with a spear shows immense bravery, making even a missed strike a mark of honor. The word 'iṉitu' (sweet or pleasant) emphasizes that true satisfaction and pride come from the magnitude of the attempt, not just the outcome.

ai.literal: Great valor, they say, is fearlessness; when one (hardship) has befallen (a foe), benevolence is further its sharp edge.
ai.translation: They say great valor is fearlessness in battle. But showing benevolence to a fallen foe is the sharp edge of that valor.
ai.modern: போர்க்களத்தில் அஞ்சாத வீரத்தை சிறந்த ஆண்மை என்று சொல்வார்கள். ஆனால் பகைவருக்கு ஒரு துன்பம் வந்தபோது அவருக்கு உதவுவது அந்த வீரத்தின் கூர்மையான ஆயுதமாகும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet defines true military greatness. While raw fearlessness in battle is the foundation of great valor, it is not the highest form. The poet states that showing benevolence and helping a defeated or struggling enemy is the sharpest edge of that bravery. This elevates physical courage into a noble, moral victory.

ai.literal: Hand-spear at elephant having thrown, he who comes body-spear having pulled out, will smile.
ai.translation: The warrior who threw his spear at an elephant and comes looking for another, pulls out a spear pierced in his own chest and smiles.
ai.modern: தன் கையிலிருந்த வேலை எதிரியின் யானை மீது வீசிவிட்டு, வேறு ஆயுதம் தேடி வருபவன், தன் மார்பில் தைத்திருக்கும் வேலைக் கண்டு அதனைப் பிடுங்கி மகிழ்ந்து சிரிப்பான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet vividly illustrates the fearless spirit of a true warrior. In the heat of battle, a soldier hurls his spear at a charging elephant and is left unarmed. Looking for another weapon to continue fighting, he finds a spear lodged in his own chest, pulls it out, and smiles in triumph. The word 'நகும்' (smiles) captures his sheer joy in finding a weapon, completely ignoring the pain of his wound.

ai.literal: Glared eyes, spear having taken to throw, destroying if blinked, defeat is it not to the brave ones?
ai.translation: If the eyes that glared fearlessly blink when a spear is hurled at them, is it not a defeat for the brave?
ai.modern: பகைவர் வேலைக் கொண்டு வீசும்போது, அவரைச் சினந்து பார்த்த கண்கள் நிலைமாறி இமைத்தால், அது வீரர்களுக்கு ஒரு தோல்வி அல்லவா?
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the absolute steadfastness expected of a true warrior. The phrase 'விழித்த கண்' refers to eyes opened wide in a fearless glare at the enemy. If those eyes blink when a spear is hurled at them, the word 'அழித்து' implies that the blink destroys their courageous stance. For the truly brave, even such an involuntary flinch is considered a retreat or defeat ('ஒட்டு').

ai.literal: Glorious-wound not-received days all, among-the-wasted he-will-place, his-own days having-taken.
ai.translation: Taking stock of his past, a warrior will count all the days he did not receive a glorious wound as wasted.
ai.modern: ஒரு வீரன் தன் வாழ்நாட்களைக் கணக்கிட்டுப் பார்த்து, அவற்றில் போர்க்களத்தில் விழுப்புண் படாத நாட்களை எல்லாம் வீணான நாட்கள் என்று கருதுவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the mindset of a true warrior. The word 'விழுப்புண்' refers to a glorious wound, specifically one received bravely on the front of the body in battle. The hero reviews his past ('தன் நாளை எடுத்து') to evaluate his life's worth. He considers any day that passed without earning such a noble wound as a day that slipped away uselessly ('வழுக்கினுள் வைக்கும்'). It highlights that for a warrior, a life of passive safety is a wasted life, while physical sacrifice in battle is the true measure of a day well lived.

ai.literal: Spreading fame desiring, not desiring life those who have, warrior's anklet fastening beauty has the nature of.
ai.translation: For warriors who desire enduring fame and disregard their own lives, fastening the battle anklet is a true adornment.
ai.modern: நிலைத்து நிற்கும் புகழை விரும்பித் தம் உயிரைப் பொருட்படுத்தாத வீரர்களுக்கு, காலில் வீரக்கழலைக் கட்டிக்கொள்வது ஒரு சிறந்த அழகாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the mindset of true warriors who value honor over survival. The phrase 'சுழலும் இசை' refers to fame that spreads and endures across the world. Because these warriors desire such glory and disregard their own lives, preparing for battle is a joyous occasion for them. Fastening the warrior's anklet is not seen as a march to death, but rather as a beautiful adornment that highlights their bravery.

ai.translation: Warriors who do not fear for their lives when battle comes will not lose their glory even if the king is angry with them.
ai.modern: போர் மூண்டால் தம் உயிருக்கு அஞ்சாத வீரர்களின் பெருமை, அரசனே அவர்கள் மீது சினம் கொண்டாலும் குறையாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the unshakeable honor of true warriors. The phrase 'உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா' describes their core trait: when battle comes, they do not fear losing their lives. Because their valor is intrinsic and self-driven, their greatness ('சீர்') does not depend on the king's favor. Even if the king ('இறைவன்') becomes angry with them ('செறினும்'), their martial glory remains undiminished.

ai.literal: What was undertaken without deviating those who die (acc.) who indeed failure those who can punish
ai.translation: Who can find fault with and punish those who die without deviating from their vow?
ai.modern: தாம் ஏற்றுக்கொண்ட சபதத்திலிருந்து விலகாமல் போர்க்களத்தில் உயிர்விடுபவர்களை, அவர்கள் தோற்றுவிட்டார்கள் என்று குற்றம் சாட்டித் தண்டிக்கக் கூடியவர் எவரும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet honors the ultimate commitment of warriors on the battlefield. The word 'iḻaittatu' refers to the solemn vow a soldier makes before battle, while 'piḻaittatu' refers to a failure or fault. If they fight to the death without retreating, they have fulfilled their vow perfectly. Therefore, even if the battle is lost, no one can punish or reproach them for failure, because their honorable death is itself a victory of their spirit.

ai.literal: Protectors' eyes tears to overflow if can die, death having begged taking fitness it has.
ai.translation: If a warrior can die in a way that brings tears to his commander's eyes, such a death is worth obtaining even by begging.
ai.modern: தம்மைப் பாதுகாக்கும் தலைவனின் கண்களில் கண்ணீர் பெருகுமாறு ஒருவரால் போர்க்களத்தில் சாக முடியுமானால், அத்தகைய மரணம் இரந்தாவது பெற்றுக்கொள்ளத் தக்க பெருமை உடையது.
ai.explanation: This couplet speaks of the ultimate glory a warrior can achieve on the battlefield. The word 'புரந்தார்' refers to the king or commander who protects the soldiers and the land. If a warrior fights so valiantly that his death brings tears of sorrow and pride to his leader's eyes ('கண் நீர் மல்க'), that death is of the highest value. The phrase 'இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து' means such a noble end is worth obtaining even by begging for it. It highlights the deep bond between the leader and the warrior, and the supreme honor of a heroic sacrifice.
